GUIDE: G'day everyone, and welcome aboard the Sea Breeze for our ninety-minute tour of Port Kirra harbour. My name's Mick, and I'll be your guide today.
Before we leave, a few safety points. Life jackets are under your seats. You don't need to wear them, but please check they're there. Also, the lower deck can get slippery, so hold onto the rails when you're moving around.
Now, the route. We'll head out past the old customs house, which was built in 1870 and is now an art gallery. Then we'll cross to the northern side of the harbour, where you'll see the naval base. Photos of the base are fine from the boat, but don't use drones — they're strictly banned anywhere in the harbour.
About halfway through, we'll stop near Shell Island. This is our best spot for dolphins. We see them on about seventy per cent of trips, so fingers crossed. If they do come close, please don't throw any food into the water. It's actually illegal, and it's bad for the dolphins.
On the way back, we'll go under the Kirra Bridge, which was the longest single-span bridge in the state when it opened. And we'll pass the fish markets, where you can buy fresh prawns if you're hungry after the tour.
The bar on the upper deck sells drinks and snacks. We've stopped selling bottled water to cut plastic, but there's a free refill station next to the bar, so do top up your bottles.
And finally, if you've booked the combined ticket, it includes entry to the maritime museum. Just show your boarding pass at the museum entrance any time in the next seven days. Righto, let's cast off.

SPEAKER: Good evening. I'm Helen Price from Brindley District Council's waste team, and I'm here to explain the changes to household collections that start on the 1st of April.
At the moment, most households have two bins: a black one for general rubbish, collected weekly, and a green one for recycling, collected every two weeks. From April, black bins will be collected every two weeks instead. I know some people are concerned about that, but our studies show that around a third of what goes in the black bin could actually be recycled.
To help, every home will receive a small brown caddy for food waste. Food waste will be collected every week, on the same day as your current black bin collection. It'll be taken to a plant outside the town, where it's turned into energy and fertiliser for local farms.
The green bin is also changing. Previously you had to separate paper from plastics and cans. From April, you can put all of these together, as the sorting will be done by machine. However, glass must now go in a separate box, which we'll deliver in March. Glass was breaking in the trucks and damaging the paper.
Garden waste, such as grass and leaves, is a separate paid service. That costs forty-five pounds a year and it isn't changing.
If you need a larger black bin, for example because you have a big family or someone in your home uses nappies, you can apply for one on the council website.
Finally, we'll be posting a calendar showing your new collection days to every household in March. Please keep it somewhere handy, like on the fridge.
question: How often will black bins be collected from April?
explanation: 週 1 回から every two weeks instead に かわる。

ANNOUNCER: Welcome to the Dalebank Steam Railway. Here's some information for today's passengers.
Our steam trains run between Dalebank and Ferncross, a distance of about nine miles. The journey takes forty minutes each way. There are three stations on the line, and you can get on and off as often as you like with your day ticket.
The first stop after Dalebank is Hollins Halt. It's a tiny station, but there's a lovely woodland walk from there down to the river. Please note it's a request stop, so tell the guard if you want to get off.
At Ferncross, the end of the line, you'll find our engine shed, where volunteers are restoring a locomotive that was built in 1924. You're welcome to watch them at work, but you must stay behind the yellow line for safety.
Today, the train you'll travel on is pulled by an engine called Lady Margaret. Unfortunately, our dining carriage is out of service for repairs, so there won't be any food on board. However, the tea room at Ferncross station is open, and it serves hot meals until two thirty.
If you'd like to see the driver at work, there are footplate experiences available, where you ride in the engine cab for part of the journey. These must be booked at the ticket office, and they're for adults only.
Also, don't miss the model railway exhibition in the old waiting room at Dalebank. It's free to enter, and children love it.
The last train back from Ferncross leaves at four fifteen. Please make sure you're on it, as there are no buses from Ferncross on Sundays. Thank you, and enjoy your journey.
question: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER. One journey takes ______ minutes.
explanation: The journey takes forty minutes each way と 言っている。nine は 距離（マイル）。

HOST: Kia ora, everyone, and welcome to Tui Lodge Backpackers. I'm Ana. I'll give you a quick rundown so you can settle in.
Reception is open from seven in the morning until ten at night. If you arrive back after ten, your key card opens the side door, not the main entrance, so remember that.
The kitchen is on the ground floor and it's shared. Every guest gets a labelled shelf in the fridge. Anything left in the fridge without a name will be thrown out on Sunday evenings. There's also a free food shelf where people leave things they don't need when they move on, so help yourself.
Laundry. The machines are in the basement. A wash costs four dollars and you can pay by card. Please don't leave clothes in the dryers overnight.
Now, activities. Lots of you will want to do the Ridgeback Track, which is a full-day hike with amazing views over the lakes. We run a shuttle to the start of the track at seven thirty each morning. It costs $35 return and you must book by six the evening before.
If the weather's bad — and it changes quickly around here — the track can close, and in that case we'll refund your shuttle fare. As an alternative, we often take people to the hot pools, about twenty minutes' drive away.
Every Wednesday night we have a barbecue in the garden. It's free for guests, you just bring your own drinks. It's a great way to meet people.
Lastly, wi-fi is free in the common room and the garden, but it doesn't reach the bedrooms, so please don't complain to us about that! The password is on the back of your key card holder.
question: After 10 pm, guests should use
explanation: your key card opens the side door, not the main entrance と 言っている。

SPEAKER: Good morning. I'm Owen Lewis, project officer for the new Greenway cycle network here in Aberford, and I'd like to tell you about the routes that open next month.
The network has three main routes, all starting from the central square. The Blue Route goes south along the old railway line to the hospital and the university. It's completely flat and separated from traffic for its whole length, which makes it ideal for beginners.
The Red Route heads east towards the industrial estate. It's mostly on quiet roads, but there's one busy roundabout where you'll need to walk your bike across using the pedestrian crossing. We're still discussing with the highways department whether a bridge can be built there.
The Green Route goes north along the canal to the village of Little Hampden. It's the most scenic, but parts of the towpath are narrow, so please ring your bell and slow down when passing walkers.
To support the network, we're installing secure bike racks at the train station, with space for two hundred bikes. These will have CCTV cameras. There'll also be a hire scheme: you'll be able to rent bikes from twelve docking points around town using a phone app. The first thirty minutes of each ride will be free.
We're also offering free cycle-training sessions for adults who haven't ridden for years and want to get their confidence back. They run on Sunday mornings in the park.
Finally, we'd love to hear your views. Paper maps will be available at the library, but the most up-to-date version will always be on our website, because we expect to make small changes in the first few months.
question: Which route is recommended for beginners?
explanation: Blue Route は 平らで 車道から 分離 → ideal for beginners と 言っている。

SPEAKER: Hello and welcome to this open evening at the Lanyard Arts Centre. I'm Jo, the courses coordinator, and I'm going to tell you about the short courses we're offering this autumn.
Let's start with pottery, which is always our most popular course. It runs on Monday and Thursday evenings for eight weeks. All materials are included, and you'll take home everything you make once it's been fired in our kiln. Places go quickly, so if you're interested, book tonight.
Next, there's a new course this year in photography. You don't need an expensive camera — in fact the tutor recommends using your phone for the first few weeks, so you can concentrate on composition rather than technical settings.
For anyone interested in writing, we have a creative writing group on Wednesday afternoons. It's aimed at retired people, but anyone who's free during the day is welcome. At the end of the course, we publish a small book of the participants' work.
We also have a printmaking course. This one's held on Saturday mornings, and it's a good choice for families, because children over ten can attend with an adult.
Now, fees. Most courses cost ninety pounds, but pottery is £110, because of the cost of the clay and firing. If you book two courses, you'll get fifteen per cent off the second one.
Our studios are on the first floor, and there's a lift. Parking is limited, so we recommend the bus. The number 6 stops right outside.
Finally, there's an exhibition of work by last year's students in the entrance hall, and tonight you can vote for your favourite piece. The winner gets a free course.

GUIDE: Good afternoon, and welcome to this walking tour of the old town of Saltmarsh. I'm Victor, and for the next two hours we'll be exploring streets that have changed remarkably little since the eighteenth century.
We're standing in Market Square, which, contrary to what many guidebooks claim, was never actually used as a market. The name comes from a family called Market who owned most of the land here. The confusion is understandable, but local historians settled the question some years ago.
From here we'll walk down Weavers Lane. The houses on the left were built for cloth workers, and you'll notice the unusually large windows on the top floors. These let in as much daylight as possible for weaving, since candles were expensive and a fire risk.
At the bottom of the lane is St Botolph's Church. Its tower leans slightly to the north. People often assume this is due to age, but surveyors have shown it was caused by a drainage channel dug beneath it in the 1800s.
After that we'll visit the old customs house on the quay. It's privately owned, so we can't go inside, but the carvings above the door are worth seeing. They show the goods that once passed through the port, mainly wool and salt.
Our final stop is the Tide Mill. This is the only surviving mill of its kind in the region, and it still grinds flour twice a month. You can buy a bag in the shop. Unfortunately, the mill wheel isn't turning today, because the tide times don't match our tour.
Please stay together, keep to the pavements, and don't hesitate to ask questions along the way.
question: Where does the name "Market Square" come from?
explanation: was never actually used as a market、名前は a family called Market から。ガイドブックの 説明は まちがい。
